Massachusetts law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there.

What the official sources say

  • Massachusetts courts quote that a claimant must show 'actual, open, exclusive, and adverse possession'; failure to establish any element is fatal. The Mass.gov law-library page lists the elements as continuous, exclusive, hostile, open, and notorious. (Massachusetts law about adverse possession (Mass.gov, Trial Court Law Libraries); source)
  • No title to registered land can be acquired through adverse possession. (M.G.L. c. 185, § 53 (cited on Mass.gov adverse possession page); source)

Massachusetts Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Massachusetts house?

Check the statute and talk to a Massachusetts attorney about your facts.

What does adverse possession mean in Massachusetts?

Adverse possession lets a person claim ownership of land they have openly used, against the true owner's wishes, for a long enough time. The Trial Court Law Libraries describe it as a doctrine that allows a person to claim a property right in land owned by another, and note it is sometimes called squatters' rights.

The law library's page gives a plain definition drawn from Black's Law Dictionary: enjoyment of real property with a claim of right, opposed to another person's claim, that is continuous, exclusive, hostile, open and notorious. The doctrine rewards productive use of land and, in the library's words, punishes owners who sleep on their rights.

Common examples on that page are steady use of a private road or driveway and farming an unused parcel. Those examples look very different from a stranger walking into a vacant house, which is a point the rest of this guide returns to.

How long must someone possess land in Massachusetts to claim it?

Twenty years. Under G.L. c. 260, section 21, an action to recover land must be brought within twenty years after the right of action or entry first accrued, or within twenty years after the claimant or those they claim under were seized or possessed of the premises.

The law library's listing adds related sections. Section 22 deals with time spent by a predecessor, which counts toward the period, and section 28 deals with open possession. A seller who inherited a house therefore needs to ask what happened on the land in earlier owners' time, not only during their own.

The Appeals Court case 1148 Davol Street LLC v. Mechanic's Mill One LLC, 86 Mass. App. Ct. 748 (2014), added that a claim against a private party can begin to accrue while the land was still publicly owned. Time can run in the background longer than owners expect.

One exception appears in section 21 itself: it does not bar an action by or on behalf of a nonprofit land conservation corporation or trust for land held for conservation, parks, recreation, water protection or wildlife protection.

What must a squatter prove?

The claimant carries the burden and must prove every element. The law library quotes Holmes v. Johnson, 324 Mass. 450 (1949), which says the burden of proof extends to all the necessary elements of such possession.

Older and newer cases on the same page set out the elements in similar words. Cook v. Babcock (1853) calls for actual, open, exclusive and adverse possession and says failure to establish any one is fatal. Ryan v. Stavros, 348 Mass. 251 (1964), puts it as nonpermissive use that is actual, open, notorious, exclusive and adverse for twenty years.

  • Open and notorious: visible enough that a reasonable owner would notice.
  • Exclusive: not shared with the owner or the public.
  • Hostile or nonpermissive: without the owner's permission. Use you allowed in writing or by word is a weak foundation for a claim.
  • Continuous for the full period.

The law library lists Miller v. Abramson, 95 Mass. App. Ct. 828 (2019), as an illustration that ordinary care can be enough. In that suburban dispute over a sliver of land, mowing and maintaining it as an average owner would supported a finding of adverse possession.

Which Massachusetts land cannot be taken by adverse possession?

Registered land, land held by the Commonwealth, and railroad property cannot be taken this way. The law library lists the three statutes that say so.

Land typeStatute listed by the law library
Registered land (Land Court Certificate of Title)G.L. c. 185, section 53
Land held by the CommonwealthG.L. c. 7C, section 32
Railroad propertyG.L. c. 160, section 88

The registered land rule is the one owners most often benefit from. Section 53 of chapter 185 says no title to registered land, or easement or other right in it against the registered owner, may be gained by prescription or adverse possession, and no right of way by necessity is implied in a conveyance of registered land. If your deed history shows a Certificate of Title, that protection applies.

Whether your parcel is registered or recorded is a title question your attorney or the registry can answer in a few minutes.

Is a squatter the same as an adverse possessor?

No. A person who walks into a vacant house is a trespasser, not someone building a twenty year claim. The law library page says directly that adverse possession is not the same as trespassing and sends readers to the trespass statute.

That statute is G.L. c. 266, section 120. It punishes someone who, without right, enters or remains in a dwelling house, building or improved or enclosed land of another after being forbidden by the person with lawful control, whether directly or by posted notice. The penalty is a fine of up to $100, or up to thirty days in jail, or both. A police officer, sheriff, deputy sheriff or constable may arrest a person found trespassing and hold them up to twenty four hours, Sunday excepted, until a complaint can be made.

The statute carries a significant limit. It does not apply to tenants or occupants of residential premises who rightfully entered at the start of a tenancy or occupancy and stay after it has ended or is alleged to have ended. For those people the owner or landlord may recover possession only through appropriate civil proceedings.

What should an owner do about an unauthorized occupant?

Document the situation, give a clear written notice that the person is not allowed to stay, and get advice before acting yourself. Which route fits depends on how the person got in, which is exactly the line section 120 draws between trespassers and people who entered with permission.

  • Someone who never had permission: forbid entry in writing or by posted notice, then involve the police under the trespass statute.
  • Someone who entered as a tenant or occupant and stayed: do not change locks or remove belongings. The statute says possession may be recovered only through civil proceedings.
  • A boundary or use dispute with a neighbor: that is a title question, and the law library lists writings on quiet title actions in the Land Court as one way owners address it.

Keep dated photographs, copies of any lease or message exchange, and utility records. They show who was in the house and under what terms, and a buyer's attorney will ask for them.

How does an occupant claim affect selling a Massachusetts house?

An open dispute over who has the right to occupy or own the land complicates a conventional sale, because a buyer's lender and title attorney need clear title and, usually, possession at closing. That is general closing practice rather than a statute, and your own attorney should confirm what applies to your property.

Deeds to recorded land are filed with the registry of deeds, and under G.L. c. 183, section 4, a conveyance is not valid against most third parties unless recorded. A claim based on long possession is a question about facts on the ground, so ask your attorney how it would show up in a title review.

If you own a house with an unresolved occupant, you can describe the situation to Cash Home Buyers and see whether an as-is purchase fits. An attorney should look at the legal side before any papers are signed.

More questions about Massachusetts Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

Can a squatter take ownership of my Massachusetts house?

Only by meeting every element for the full twenty years. G.L. c. 260, section 21 sets the period, and the claimant must prove actual, open, notorious, exclusive and adverse possession without permission. A short stay does not qualify.

How many years does adverse possession take in Massachusetts?

Twenty years under G.L. c. 260, section 21. Time spent by a predecessor in possession can count toward that period under section 22.

Can adverse possession happen on registered land?

No. G.L. c. 185, section 53 says no title to registered land can be acquired by prescription or adverse possession.

Can I remove a squatter myself?

If the person is a trespasser who never had permission, the police can act under G.L. c. 266, section 120. If the person entered as a tenant or occupant, the same section says possession can be recovered only through civil proceedings, so do not use self help.

Is trespassing a crime in Massachusetts?

Yes. Section 120 sets a fine up to $100, up to thirty days in jail, or both, once a person is forbidden to be on the property and stays or returns.

Does adverse possession apply to government land?

No. The law library lists G.L. c. 7C, section 32 for Commonwealth land and G.L. c. 160, section 88 for railroad property as barring adverse possession.

Massachusetts statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold.

What the official sources say

  • At or before tenancy start a landlord may not require more than first month's rent, last month's rent at the same rate, and a security deposit equal to the first month's rent. (M.G.L. c. 186, § 15B(1)(b); source)
  • If the landlord fails to comply with certain deposit duties, the tenant is awarded three times the deposit plus 5% interest from when payment was due, plus court costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Tenant must get a receipt at the time of the deposit and, within 30 days, a receipt naming the bank and account. (M.G.L. c. 186, § 15B(3)(b), (7); source)
  • Where rent is paid monthly in a tenancy at will, either party may end it with notice of 30 days or one month before the next rent due date, whichever is longer; rent can change with notice on the same terms. (Attorney General's Guide to Landlord and Tenant Rights; source)
  • Landlord must arrange with the tenant in advance to enter to repair, inspect or show the unit; entry without approval is allowed only for an emergency with potential to damage the whole building, or apparent abandonment. (Attorney General's Guide to Landlord and Tenant Rights; source)
  • Landlord must provide a unit compliant with the Massachusetts State Sanitary Code (105 CMR 410) and maintain it in habitable condition throughout the tenancy. (Attorney General's Guide to Landlord and Tenant Rights; source)
  • Certain landlord conduct within six months of a tenant's protected activity (e.g., reporting Sanitary Code violations) is presumed retaliatory. (Attorney General's Guide to Landlord and Tenant Rights; source)
  • No lease may impose interest or a penalty for late rent until 30 days after the rent is due. (M.G.L. c. 186, § 15B(1)(c); source)
Selling in Massachusetts?

Get My Cash Offer →

What kinds of tenancy exist in Massachusetts?

Massachusetts recognizes two main kinds of tenancy: a lease for a fixed term and a tenancy-at-will. The Attorney General's guide says the rights of both landlord and tenant depend partly on which one was created, so the first job for any owner thinking about a sale is to work out which one the renter actually has.

With a lease, the rent stays the same for the term, usually one year, and the landlord cannot end the tenancy unless the tenant fails to meet the lease conditions. A tenancy-at-will lasts until either side properly ends it. Many people call it month-to-month, and sometimes there is no written agreement at all.

Where rent is paid monthly, either side ends an at-will tenancy by giving notice of 30 days or one month before the next rent due date, whichever is longer. Rent can change on the same notice. A tenant who pays weekly is also at will, and the termination notice rule stays the same.

What can a Massachusetts landlord collect at the start of a tenancy?

A landlord may ask for only four things up front: first month's rent, a security deposit, last month's rent, and the actual cost of a new lock and key. The deposit cannot be more than one month's rent.

Up-front itemWhat the Attorney General's guide says
First month's rentAllowed
Security depositCovers damage beyond normal wear and tear, capped at one month's rent
Last month's rentAllowed, with a signed receipt
Lock and keyOnly the actual cost of a new lock and key
Pet, broker or application feesNot allowed at the start of a tenancy

The guide also notes a law that took effect on August 1, 2025. It bars brokers and salespeople from charging tenants fees when they mainly serve the landlord, and a landlord still cannot pass on a fee for a broker's work for the landlord.

How must a landlord handle a security deposit?

The deposit goes into an interest-bearing account at a Massachusetts bank within the first month of the tenancy, kept apart from the landlord's own money. The tenant is entitled to the bank's name and address and the account number.

  • Each year the landlord either pays the interest to the tenant or lets the tenant deduct it from rent.
  • A statement of condition is due within 10 days of the tenancy start or of receiving the deposit, whichever is later, and the tenant then has 15 days to add to it.
  • At move-out the deposit plus interest comes back within 30 days.
  • If the landlord keeps part of it for damage, a written description and a repair estimate are due within 30 days of move-out.

For an owner who plans to sell a rented house, these records matter. The guide sets detailed duties around the deposit, so gather the receipts, the bank details and the statement of condition before you talk to any buyer.

Can a landlord show a rented house to buyers?

Yes, but only by arrangement. The guide says the landlord must arrange with the tenant in advance to enter the unit to make repairs, inspect it, or show it to prospective tenants, buyers or real estate agents.

Entry without approval is limited to two situations: a mechanical or repair emergency with the potential to damage the whole building, or an apparent abandonment of the apartment. A planned showing for a buyer is neither of those. If you sell with a tenant in place, expect to schedule every visit around the renter.

That is one reason owners with occupied rentals sometimes prefer a buyer who will purchase as-is without repeated walk-throughs. It is also a reason to keep communication with the tenant calm and in writing.

What repair duties continue while the house is for sale?

The landlord must keep the unit habitable for the whole tenancy, and listing the house for sale does not change that. The State Sanitary Code, 105 CMR 410, sets the minimum standards, and the right to habitable housing covers every occupant, not only the named tenant.

If a landlord does not respond, a tenant can ask a code enforcement officer or the local board of health to inspect, and an inspector can order the landlord to fix violations. The guide says a tenant who cannot get repairs may in some cases withhold part of the rent or move out, and it advises talking to a lawyer or legal services first.

Lead paint adds another layer. For a rental built before 1978, landlord and tenant must sign and keep the Tenant Lead Law Notification and Tenant Certification. If a child under six will live there, the landlord must delead or bring the hazards under interim control, and cannot refuse to rent to a family with young children because of lead.

What counts as retaliation, and why does it matter before a sale?

Retaliation is any threat or reprisal against a tenant or occupant for using a legal right. A rushed sale plan can look like retaliation if it follows a tenant's complaint, so the timing deserves care.

Protected activity includes reporting conditions to the landlord or the board of health, filing a complaint in court or with an agency, and joining a tenants' union. The guide lists examples of illegal reprisals:

  • Raising the rent or refusing to renew a lease.
  • Changing the locks or shutting off heat or electricity.
  • Starting an eviction.
  • Reporting a tenant to the police or to immigration officials.
  • Harassing a tenant or other occupant.

Certain landlord conduct within six months of a tenant's protected activity is presumed retaliatory. In a lawsuit, a court would assume the action was a reprisal unless the landlord proves otherwise.

Which lease terms are illegal in Massachusetts?

A lease cannot contain several terms that landlords sometimes copy from old forms. The Attorney General's guide names these as illegal:

  • Making the tenant pay to repair ordinary wear and tear.
  • Requiring professional cleaning at the end of the lease.
  • Making the tenant pay for repairs to parts of the building outside the apartment.
  • Barring the tenant from suing the landlord or reporting Sanitary Code violations.
  • Barring the tenant from joining a tenants' union.
  • Charging a late fee when rent is less than 30 days late.

A lease must also name the owner, the person responsible for maintenance, and the person who accepts formal notices, with addresses and phone numbers. If the landlord holds a deposit, the lease must show the amount and explain the tenant's rights to it. Check your own lease against this list before you share it with anyone.

How does eviction work if you need the house empty?

A Massachusetts landlord cannot remove a tenant without a court's permission. Physically removing the tenant or their belongings, or changing the locks, is not allowed.

The usual path starts with a notice, most often a Notice to Quit, whose length depends on the tenancy type and the reason. The landlord then files a Summary Process case, which begins when the tenant is served a Summons and Complaint. The tenant can raise defenses such as improper termination, uncorrected known problems, retaliation, or discrimination, including a failure to grant a reasonable accommodation.

If the landlord wins, the court issues a judgment and then an execution, which lets a sheriff or constable carry out a physical eviction. The tenant's property goes to a licensed public warehouse, the landlord pays the moving fees and is entitled to reimbursement, and the tenant gets one opportunity to claim items of personal or sentimental value. Because the process takes time, owners who need to sell quickly often weigh it against a sale to a buyer who accepts the tenant in place.

What does a seller of a one or two family home need from the fire department?

You need a certificate of compliance showing your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the rules for a sale or transfer. The Department of Fire Services says to call the local fire department as soon as you have a closing date.

The requirements depend on when the home was built and when the last building permit was issued. Battery-powered smoke alarms more than 10 years old, or expired, must be replaced with 10-year sealed units that are photoelectric and have a hush feature. An alarm with no manufacture date counts as expired. The fire department charges a fee, so ask the local office what it is.

What should a landlord do before selling a tenant-occupied house?

Start by confirming the tenancy type and any lease end date, then gather the deposit records and any repair complaints. The official guide does not say how an existing lease or at-will tenancy is treated when the property changes hands, so ask a Massachusetts real estate attorney before you sign anything.

The Attorney General's Consumer Hotline at (617) 727-8400 answers general questions about the guide, and a local board of health can explain Sanitary Code issues. When you are ready to talk about a sale, bring the lease, rent ledger, deposit receipts and any inspection notices.

More questions about Massachusetts Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in Massachusetts?

Either side must give notice of 30 days or one month before the next rent due date, whichever is longer, according to the Attorney General's guide. The same timing applies to a rent change.

Can a Massachusetts landlord keep a security deposit for normal wear and tear?

No. A landlord may keep unpaid rent and the cost of damage beyond normal wear and tear, and must return the rest with interest within 30 days. A lease may not make the tenant pay for ordinary wear.

Can I enter a rented house to show it to a buyer without asking?

No. The landlord must arrange the visit with the tenant in advance. Entry without approval is allowed only for an emergency that could damage the whole building or an apparent abandonment.

Do I need court approval to evict a tenant before I sell?

Yes. A landlord cannot evict by removing the tenant, removing belongings or changing locks. The landlord gives proper notice, files a summary process case, and only a sheriff or constable carries out a physical eviction after a judgment and execution.

What do I need from the fire department to sell a one or two family home?

A certificate of compliance showing your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the requirements for a sale or transfer. Call the local fire department when you have a closing date and ask about its fee.

Massachusetts Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Massachusetts law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason.

What the official sources say

  • A notice to quit gives 14 days (nonpayment) or 30 days (other reasons) before the landlord may go to court; a notice to quit is required before filing summary process. (Tenants' guide to eviction (Mass.gov); source)
  • Landlords can file in a District Court or Housing Court. (Tenants' guide to eviction (Mass.gov); source)
  • Tenant has 10 days from entry of judgment to appeal; the landlord can hire a sheriff or constable 11 days after the final decision; the officer must give written notice 2 days (excluding weekends/holidays) before removal; removals only Monday-Friday 9 a.m.-5 p.m. and the execution must be used within 3 months. (Tenants' guide to eviction (Mass.gov); source)
  • Officer removes tenant's belongings to a licensed storage facility; tenant may owe storage fees. (Tenants' guide to eviction (Mass.gov); source)
Selling in Massachusetts?
We buy Massachusetts houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What notice does a Massachusetts landlord have to give before filing an eviction?

A Massachusetts landlord has to end the tenancy with a written notice to quit before any court case can begin. The state's tenants' guide to eviction says a landlord must send this notice first, and that receiving one does not mean the tenant has to leave right away. Only a court order can force a move.

The number of days depends on the reason and on the kind of tenancy. This page covers each version, how a notice has to be delivered, and what it means for an owner who plans to sell the house.

How many days does each Massachusetts notice to quit give?

Fourteen days applies to unpaid rent, and thirty days is the usual figure for most other reasons. The table sets out the versions described by the state's court and housing pages.

SituationWritten noticeSource
Rent not paid14 days, unless the lease says otherwiseMassachusetts Court System landlord guide; G.L. c. 186, section 12
Rent not paid, federally assisted housingA 30-day notice may be usedMass.gov tenants' guide
Month-to-month tenancy at willAt least 30 days, ending at the close of a rental periodCourt System landlord guide
Lease violation or landlord wants the unit back30 daysMass.gov tenants' guide
Lease that has run outNo notice needed, since the lease sets the end dateCourt System landlord guide

The statute for a tenancy at will reads a little differently from the plain summary. It speaks of three months' notice, and when rent is paid at shorter intervals the notice must equal the gap between payment days or thirty days, whichever is longer. A gap between rent dates that runs longer than thirty days can therefore stretch the notice.

Can a tenant stop a 14-day nonpayment notice by paying?

Sometimes. Under G.L. c. 186, section 12, a tenant who has not received a similar notice in the previous twelve months keeps the tenancy by paying or tendering the full rent due within ten days after receiving the notice.

Every nonpayment notice must carry a short statement telling the tenant about this right. If the statement is missing, the tenant's time to pay stretches to the day the answer is due in a court case, though the omission does not otherwise ruin the notice. When a late payment traces back to a delay by a federal, state or municipal agency, the court must continue the hearing at least seven days and can treat the tenancy as never terminated if everything owed is tendered.

Mass.gov describes paying arrears by an agreed date as "curing" the problem. Other points it lists for nonpayment cases:

  • The RAFT program offers emergency payments of up to $7,000 per year to eligible households behind on rent.
  • A tenant with a pending RAFT application cannot be evicted, and should tell the court about it.
  • A landlord must attach a form listing rental assistance programs to a nonpayment notice.
  • A payment plan negotiated with the landlord can also stop the case from moving forward.

What does a valid notice to quit have to contain?

A valid notice names the exact day the tenancy ends and, for most reasons, states why the landlord is ending it. The Court System guide stresses that the notice exists to end the tenancy, so the tenant must actually receive it for it to work.

  • A written notice, except where a lease simply expires.
  • The specific date on which the tenancy will end.
  • The reason, when the cause is a lease violation or unpaid rent.
  • The statutory right-to-pay statement, for nonpayment.
  • The rental assistance form, for nonpayment.

No single delivery method is required. A landlord can hand the notice to the tenant, and the guide recommends having a disinterested person present. Two common shortcuts fail: a constable leaving the notice at the tenant's last usual address when the tenant never actually receives it, and a mailed notice the tenant does not pick up. Sample forms are available through the Trial Court Law Libraries, with a warning that they may not be legally sufficient in every case.

Why does the calendar matter, especially around February?

Because a month-to-month notice has to expire at the end of a rental period, the date it is served decides when the tenancy can end. The Court System guide gives one example: a notice served too late in January cannot end the tenancy by March 1, since February is shorter than thirty days.

An older notice does not always have to be repeated. A landlord who served a notice months ago generally does not need a new one, unless the right to evict was waived, for example by accepting rent in advance without a written reservation of rights, or by signing a new rental agreement that created a fresh tenancy. Owners who have taken a late rent payment since serving notice should ask an attorney whether the notice still stands.

What is a landlord not allowed to do while the notice runs?

A landlord cannot lock the tenant out, shut off services or use force to regain the home. Both the tenants' guide and the state statute say only a judge's order can remove a tenant.

Under G.L. c. 186, section 14, a landlord who willfully fails to supply water, heat, light, power or gas, interferes with quiet enjoyment, or tries to regain possession by force without judicial process faces a fine of $25 to $300 or up to six months in jail. The tenant can also recover actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.

The Court System guide adds that a landlord cannot evict for illegal reasons, such as a tenant reporting violations to health inspectors or withholding rent because of bad conditions.

How does a notice to quit change when the owner wants to sell the house?

Selling does not shorten anything. The tenants' guide says a no-fault notice to quit can be used because the landlord wants to sell the property, but it still means the landlord plans to take the tenant to court, and the case still appears on the tenant's housing record.

A sale also carries obligations that follow the tenancy. Under section 15B of the same chapter:

  • A landlord who transfers the building, whether by sale or otherwise, must pass the security deposit and its accrued interest to the new owner.
  • The new owner must tell the tenant in writing within forty-five days that the deposit was transferred.
  • If the old owner fails to transfer it, the new owner becomes liable for the deposit anyway.
  • Rent paid in advance for the last month must likewise be credited to the buyer, who must give notice within forty-five days.
  • A lease can allow the landlord to enter to show the home to a prospective purchaser.

These rules suggest that Massachusetts expects a tenancy to continue across a sale unless it is properly ended. An owner thinking of selling a rented house should ask a real estate attorney how a lease or tenancy at will carries over before listing.

What do owners of rented Massachusetts houses usually run into?

Most problems come from a notice that is late, incomplete or served in a way the tenant never actually received. A notice the tenant never actually received does not count as adequate notice under the Court System guide, which matters most when a closing date is already set.

  • Special rules apply to mobile home parks, rooming houses, dormitories, residential superintendents and public housing.
  • Government-subsidized rent may require the notice to state specific reasons, so the lease and program rules both need checking.
  • The second step after an expired notice is a summary process summons and complaint, which a constable or sheriff must serve.
  • Free mediation is available through the Community Mediation Centers, and most courts offer it as well.

Some owners choose to sell the house with the tenant still living in it. Others settle on a move-out date by agreement, which the tenants' guide describes as an option when a landlord offers a little extra time. Either route should be written down and reviewed by a lawyer.

More questions about Massachusetts Eviction Notice Rules

How many days is a Massachusetts eviction notice?

It is 14 days for unpaid rent and 30 days for most other reasons, according to the Mass.gov tenants' guide. A month-to-month tenancy at will needs at least 30 days, ending at the close of a rental period, and the statute can call for more when rent dates are further apart.

Does a notice to quit mean the tenant has to leave?

No. A notice to quit is only the first step. The tenant can stay until a court orders otherwise, and a landlord cannot change the locks or remove belongings before then.

Can a landlord send a notice because the house is being sold?

Yes. Mass.gov describes this as a no-fault notice to quit. It still leads to a court case if the tenant does not leave, and the sale does not cancel the tenant's rights in the meantime.

Does the notice have to be mailed or hand delivered?

No single method is required, but the tenant must actually receive it. A notice left at an old address, or mailed and never picked up, is not adequate notice.

What happens to the security deposit when a rented house is sold?

The seller must transfer the deposit and accrued interest to the buyer, and the buyer must notify the tenant in writing within forty-five days. A buyer remains liable for the deposit even if the seller fails to transfer it.

Where can a tenant or owner get free help with a notice?

The Community Mediation Centers offer free pre-court mediation, the Court Service Centers help people without lawyers, and the Legal Resource Finder lists legal aid programs. Owners with a pending sale may also want a private real estate attorney.
